name: Kang-Petrov Arms KPA-20 'Reach'
description:
The KPA-20 stretches the KPA-16 platform to a 20-inch government-profile barrel, recovering the velocity that shorter carbines sacrifice and pushing effective engagement distance out to a genuine 500 meters with good ammunition. The gas system returns to a rifle-length direct impingement arrangement, which cycles more softly than the carbine-length system and produces less felt recoil under sustained fire. The result is a rifle that is unambiguously a rifle — not a carbine trying to be a rifle — with the handling characteristics that implies. It's heavier, longer, and less convenient in tight spaces, but it hits harder at range and the longer sight radius is forgiving of imperfect technique. The trigger is the same mil-spec two-stage unit as the KPA-16, installed in a full-length lower with a fixed A2-style stock that Kang-Petrov stubbornly refuses to replace with something adjustable despite twenty years of customer feedback.

The KPA-20 is bought by a specific type of Tier 1–2 customer: people who expect to fight at range and have decided that convenience is someone else's priority. Outer-ring community defense forces operating in open terrain, agricultural cooperative security in the GLMZ's edge zones where sight lines extend past what carbines are optimized for, and the occasional seriously-minded shelf worker who has read enough about terminal ballistics to care about velocity at distance. It doesn't sell as well as the KPA-16 — most buyers prioritize maneuverability — but its devotees are loyal.

The fixed A2 stock is a source of ongoing cultural tension around the KPA-20. Kang-Petrov's official position is that the fixed stock is more durable and more accurate as a shooting platform. The unofficial position, which circulates in GLMZ armorer communities, is that the fixed stock is cheaper to produce and Slagworks allocates the cost savings elsewhere in the receiver. Both things can be true simultaneously. Operators who have adapted to it shoot the KPA-20 well. Operators who haven't adapted curse the fixed stock loudly and regularly.
specifications:
caliber: 5.56mm Combat Standard
effective_range: 500m
rate_of_fire: Semi-automatic
magazine_capacity: 30 rounds
weight: 3.6 kg
tactical_use: The KPA-20 is a deliberate rifleman's tool designed for engagements where range matters. Operators running this platform are typically positioned to cover open ground, elevated positions, or perimeter security roles where the extra barrel length translates to meaningful performance gains. It's a poor choice for close-quarters work — the length and weight become liabilities in tight corridors — but in the hands of a patient operator behind a good optic, the 20-inch barrel recovers roughly 10% of the velocity lost in carbine-length configurations, and at 400–500 meters that difference is measurable in terminal effect.
cultural_context: The KPA-20 occupies a niche in GLMZ's outer zones that nobody else quite fills at Tier 1 pricing. Agricultural edge-zone security, who operate in terrain that doesn't resemble the dense urban corridors of the inner GLMZ, prize it for the same reasons the inner-city crowd ignores it: range, precision, and the willingness to commit to a longer, heavier platform. In those communities, carrying a full-length rifle is a statement about your operating environment and your seriousness. In the inner zones, it reads as anachronistic. Context is everything.
story_hooks: A KPA-20 with a custom 6x fixed optic and a hand-loaded ammunition supply is recovered from a sniper hide overlooking a Slagworks Industrial water reclamation facility — the hide shows evidence of occupation over multiple days, the shots were never fired, and the operator vanished without their weapon, which is the kind of detail that suggests something interrupted a very patient plan.

An outer-ring community defense coordinator is asking discreet questions about whether KPA-20 rifles can be legally transferred between communities without passing through a Slagworks Industrial registration point — they have a surplus and a neighbor community that needs them, but the registration infrastructure between their zones runs through a Tessera Corponation transit corridor that charges per-item transit fees that make the transfer economically impossible through legal channels.
